concept.title: DBMS vs File System, DBMS vs RDBMS
concept.subject: Database Management Systems
prerequisites: Basic idea of data, files and tables
learningObjectives: Explain at least five problems of file-based data management that a DBMS solves
Distinguish a DBMS from a file system in terms of redundancy, access, integrity, concurrency, recovery and security
Define an RDBMS and state what the relational model adds on top of a general DBMS
Compare DBMS and RDBMS using precise (not oversimplified) criteria
Decide, given a scenario, whether a file system, a general DBMS or an RDBMS is the appropriate choice
keySkillsGained: Justifying why a DBMS is used
Answering the classic interview comparison questions

oneLineDefinition.dbms: A DBMS is software that lets you define, store, query, update and protect a shared collection of data, so applications do not manage raw files themselves.
oneLineDefinition.fileSystem: A file system stores data as separate files, and each application decides the format and the logic to read and write them.
oneLineDefinition.rdbms: An RDBMS is a DBMS built on the relational model: data lives in tables (relations) of rows and columns, linked through keys and queried with SQL.

coreIdea: File system: the OS stores and finds files, but it knows nothing about what is inside them. Meaning, rules and format live in application code.
DBMS: the data and its rules (structure, constraints, access control) live in one managed layer that every application shares.
RDBMS: a DBMS that uses one specific model, the relational model. DBMS is the broad category and RDBMS is a type within it.

keyTerms.meaning: The same data stored in multiple places.
Copies of the same data disagree, usually after one copy is updated and others are not.
Changing how data is stored or structured without rewriting the applications that use it.
A rule the data must always satisfy (e.g. unique ID, age > 0, valid foreign key).
A group of operations treated as one all-or-nothing unit.
A set of rows (tuples) with the same columns (attributes).
Attribute(s) that identify rows (primary key) or link tables (foreign key).
A declarative way to ask for data (SQL for relational systems).

mentalModel.analogy: File system is a room full of loose paper folders where every employee invents their own filing rules. DBMS is a records office with a clerk, one set of rules, a lock on the door and a log of every change. RDBMS is a records office that insists every record be a row in a standard form and that forms reference each other by ID.
mentalModel.memoryHook: File system = storage only. DBMS = storage + management. RDBMS = management using tables and relationships.

importantRules: Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but not every DBMS is an RDBMS.
A file system provides storage and retrieval of files. It does not provide query processing, transactions or constraint enforcement.
In a file system, constraints and access logic are written inside each application, so changing a file format forces changing every program that reads it.
A DBMS reduces and controls redundancy. It does not eliminate it. Replication, indexes and denormalization are deliberate redundancy.
The relational model adds: tables, keys, relationships via foreign keys, a standard language (SQL), and integrity rules over those structures.
Non-relational systems (document, key-value, graph, hierarchical, network) are DBMSs but not RDBMSs.

comparisonTables.title: File System vs DBMS
rows: Redundancy and consistency
Same data duplicated across files, copies drift apart
Data kept centrally, redundancy controlled, consistency enforced
Data access
Write a new program for each new question
Ask ad hoc questions with a query language
Data independence
Programs depend on file format and layout
Storage changes do not force application changes
Integrity
Rules hard-coded in each application, easy to miss or conflict
Rules declared once (keys, constraints) and enforced for all users
Atomicity of updates
A crash mid-update can leave data half-changed
Transactions: all-or-nothing, with recovery after failure
Concurrent access
Simultaneous writes can overwrite each other
Concurrency control (locking, isolation) keeps results correct
Security
Mostly file-level permissions from the OS
Fine-grained control per user, table, view or operation
Cost and complexity
Cheap and simple, fine for small or single-user needs
Needs software, design and administration, pays off as data and users grow

comparisonTables.title: DBMS vs RDBMS
rows: Scope
Any software managing databases, any data model
A DBMS specifically based on the relational model
Data model
Hierarchical, network, document, key-value, graph, relational, ...
Relations (tables) of rows and columns
Relationships
Model dependent (pointers, links, nesting, edges)
Expressed through keys, mainly primary and foreign keys
Query language
Varies by system
SQL (standardized)
Integrity
Varies by system
Entity and referential integrity, domain and other constraints
Schema design
Varies, may be flexible or schema-less
Typically schema-first, normalization used to reduce redundancy
Transactions
Varies, not guaranteed in every DBMS
Typically ACID transactions
Examples
MongoDB, Redis, Neo4j, IMS (hierarchical), plus relational systems
MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite

workedExample.scenario: A college stores student data in two text files: students.txt (ID, name, department name) and marks.txt (ID, name, department name, subject, marks). A department is renamed from 'CSE' to 'Computer Science'.
fileSystemWalkthrough: The department name is stored in many rows across both files (redundancy).
A program updates students.txt but crashes before updating marks.txt, so the two files now disagree (inconsistency, no atomicity).
Asking 'average marks per department' needs a new program, because no query language exists (difficult access).
Nothing stops a marks row for an ID that is not in students.txt (integrity enforced only if every program remembers to check).
dbmsWalkthrough: Store departments once and reference them by ID, so the rename is a single update.
The update runs in a transaction, so either everything changes or nothing does.
'Average marks per department' is one query.
A foreign key constraint rejects marks for non-existent students.
workedExample.rdbmsAngle: In an RDBMS, the same design is three tables: Department(dept_id PK, name), Student(student_id PK, name, dept_id FK), Marks(student_id FK, subject, marks). The foreign keys are the relationships and SQL joins them back together.
workedExample.takeaway: The DBMS did not magically change the data. It moved the rules from scattered application code into one managed layer.

importantDiagram.note: V1 shows applications tied to separate files vs sharing one DBMS. V2 shows DBMS as the broad category with RDBMS nested inside it.

commonMistakes: Saying a DBMS removes redundancy completely. Correct: it controls and minimizes it.
Saying a file system 'cannot store data properly'. Correct: it stores files fine, the weakness is lack of management features (query, constraints, transactions, concurrency control).
Listing the file system problems without linking each problem to the DBMS feature that solves it.
Treating DBMS and RDBMS as unrelated or as equal. RDBMS is a subset of DBMS.
Saying 'DBMS cannot have tables'. Correct: tables are the relational way of organizing data, other models organize data differently.
Saying RDBMS = 'uses SQL' only. The defining part is the relational model; SQL is the language that comes with it.
Mixing up 'database' (the data) and 'DBMS' (the software managing it).

interviewTraps.trap: 'Is MySQL a DBMS or an RDBMS?'
interviewTraps.answer: Both. It is a DBMS because it manages databases, and an RDBMS because it uses the relational model.
Yes, a document-oriented DBMS. It is not an RDBMS because it is not based on the relational model.
Files work for small, single-user, simple cases. Once you need shared access, consistency, queries, recovery and security, you would end up rebuilding a DBMS in application code.

interviewTraps.trap: 'DBMS stores data in files, so what is the difference from a file system?'
interviewTraps.answer: A DBMS may use files internally, but it adds a management layer on top (query processing, transactions, concurrency, recovery, constraints, security). The application never touches the files directly.

interviewTraps.trap: Textbook tables often say 'DBMS: single user, no relationships; RDBMS: multi-user, relationships'.
interviewTraps.answer: That describes old desktop or file-based DBMSs. Modern DBMSs, relational or not, support many users, so contrast on data model and relational features rather than on 'single vs multi-user'.

quickRecall.title: Remember these 5 things
points: File system = stores files only. Rules and logic sit in application code, which causes redundancy, inconsistency, hard access, weak integrity, no atomicity and unsafe concurrency.
DBMS = shared, managed data with a query language, constraints, transactions, concurrency control, recovery and security.
Data independence is a key DBMS benefit: change storage without changing applications.
RDBMS = DBMS + relational model (tables, keys, SQL, relational integrity).
Every RDBMS is a DBMS, not every DBMS is an RDBMS (e.g. MongoDB, Neo4j).

cheatSheet.oneMinuteRevision: Files store data, but each program must handle format, rules and safety itself, so you get duplicates, mismatched copies, one-off programs for every question, missing checks, half-finished updates and clashes between users. A DBMS pulls all of that into one managed layer shared by every application: queries, constraints, transactions, concurrency control, recovery, security and data independence. An RDBMS is a DBMS that organizes data as tables connected by keys and queried with SQL. So: file system < DBMS, and RDBMS is one kind of DBMS.

visuals.title: Separate files per application vs shared DBMS
visuals.purpose: Show why scattered files cause redundancy and why a central DBMS layer fixes it.
visuals.placement: After the comparison table T1 or the worked example
visuals.takeaway: In a file system each application owns its data. In a DBMS all applications go through one managed layer.
visuals.accessibilityDescription: Two side-by-side diagrams. Left: three applications each connected directly to their own file, with a duplicate 'Department' label appearing in two files. Right: the same three applications connected to a single DBMS box, which connects to one shared database.

visuals.title: Where RDBMS sits inside DBMS
visuals.takeaway: RDBMS is one kind of DBMS, not a competitor to it.
visuals.accessibilityDescription: A large rounded box labelled DBMS containing a smaller box labelled RDBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) and other boxes labelled Document (MongoDB), Key-Value (Redis), Graph (Neo4j) and Hierarchical (IMS).
